title: These 3 Things Will Kill Your Deal Right Before Closing
content: I'm Sarah Sharp, a deal attorney who helps people buy and sell businesses every day, mainly accounting practices. And I am in the midst of my biggest deal season. So, I'm going to tell you the three things that kill deals even after you've drafted the purchase agreement. Kind of on the 50ard line, right? And that was the case with all three of these deals that died this week. And it's very rare for me to have any deal die after a purchase agreement. So I'm reflecting on how it could be avoided and why it happened. So the first thing that kills deals of the three, the first thing that kills deals after you've drafted the purchase agreements and you've gone through diligence is pretty simple and unfortunately pretty unavoidable. And that is something new happens, right? So whether that's somebody being sued or somebody having a data breach or a key employee quitting, that kind of thing can come up at any time. And when it happens, it doesn't matter if you've run the most clean, perfect deal ever. It's still probably the right time to walk away if you're the buyer. And if you're the seller, unfortunately, it's going to be hard to convince somebody to move forward with you, right? So, it's not always that the thing is of an enormous magnitude, per se. So something completely unavoidable, surprising comes up. So, that is a good reason for a deal to die. And usually if a deal dies for those reasons, it's partially at least because they had a provision in your purchase agreement and they made the person promise that those things aren't true. Because what you don't want is to not have a reason for the seller to tell you about those new bad outcomes. Right? So, our purchase agreements always say, you know, I promise I'm not being sued. So, if you've got those promises, then all of a sudden you're asking the seller to sign, they're going to really hesitate when all of a sudden that happens. And in all of the cases where I've had that happen, that is what susted it out. It wasn't the seller that wanted to disclose the new thing. It was the fact that they were going to have to sign the purchase agreement that promised that thing wasn't true that made it come up. So, you know, say what you will about a deal that doesn't make it all the way through to closing. And if there's some huge data breach that you don't have the ability to get your arms around or if there's some lawsuit that's going to take who knows how long to resolve, you know, that's probably not the right deal to do then. description:
Even after a deal is deep in the legal phase, with purchase agreements drafted and diligence completed, things can still fall apart—and fast.

In this video,  break down three of the most common reasons business transactions (especially in the accounting space) die after the heavy lifting is done:

✅ Unavoidable last-minute surprises like lawsuits, data breaches, or key staff departures
✅ Over-lawyering that slows momentum or overwhelms already-busy sellers
✅ Disagreements on deal terms that surface late in negotiations

If you're buying or selling a business—especially an accounting firm—these are the landmines you need to watch out for. I’ll also share how strong reps and warranties in your purchase agreement can save your butt (and possibly your bank account).

For more information on Deal Academy, a program that teaches you how to buy and sell accounting practices, click the link here: https://www.dealacademy.org
